planting.note: Direct-sow in fall onto lean, rocky, fast-draining mineral soil in full sun; source seed specifically labeled ssp. glandulosus from a native-plant nursery given the complex's several narrow-endemic rare subspecies.

directions: The widest-ranging jewelflower, from the Northern California Coast Ranges into southwest Oregon, this species tolerates both serpentine and ordinary rocky soils, making it a forgiving entry point into the genus for native-plant gardeners who don't have true serpentine substrate. It produces the classic inflated, urn-shaped calyces in a wide color range from white to purple to near-black on tall stems. It self-sows readily once established and does not need serpentine specifically, making it more tractable than most of its relatives.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall onto true serpentine soil, or at minimum a lean, mineral, well-drained substrate with no added organic fertility; afternoon part-shade from an oak canopy is tolerated.

directions: A genuinely unusual teaching and collector plant, this species is one of only two California plants known to hyperaccumulate nickel from serpentine soil at thousands of parts per million in its tissue, which also appears to deter insect herbivores — a conversation piece for a dedicated serpentine or geobotany-themed native bed. Much of its chemical ecology depends on accessible heavy-metal content, so it tends to be outcompeted or simply fail in ordinary garden loam. Source from the one specialty native nursery that carries it rather than wild populations, which are restricted to scattered serpentine outcrops.

planting.note: Direct-sow September through March onto dry, rocky desert slopes; keep well-watered through winter and spring, unlike the California serpentine jewelflowers that want to stay dry.

directions: The jewelflower for a desert-Southwest or Chihuahuan and Sonoran themed native garden rather than a California serpentine bed, this widespread, non-endemic species carries showy bell-shaped flowers from white and cream to maroon or yellow depending on population, and serves as a nectar and larval host plant for the sara orangetip butterfly. Unlike the California serpentine jewelflowers it wants consistent moisture through winter and spring and will decline once summer heat and drought arrive. Plant it with other Chihuahuan and Sonoran desert annuals rather than alongside the California serpentine species, since the two groups have different soil and water profiles.

planting.note: Direct-sow seed thickly in a drift in fall onto lean, rocky, unamended serpentine or serpentine-adjacent soil, since the ornamental effect depends on a colony rather than scattered single plants.

directions: One of the most ornamentally showy jewelflowers, this species carries large, shiny dark-purple sterile bracts topping the stem, with paler true flowers secondary to the display, most effective massed in a colony. Native to grassland and chaparral openings on serpentine in the Inner Central Coast Ranges, it is on the conservation watch list but genuinely sold as seed by a specialty native-seed retailer, which is unusual for this genus. Seed availability is intermittent, so buy opportunistically when listed rather than counting on year-round stock.

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall onto lean, sharply drained metamorphic or slate gravel with some dappled shade, rather than baking open sun; avoid rich garden beds.

directions: Another bract-forward ornamental type, this jewelflower carries shiny red-violet to navy-blue sterile bracts up to four inches long over small white true flowers, described by its own seed retailer as easy to grow. Native to sparsely vegetated, rocky metamorphic and slate gravels in oak-pine woodland in the southern Sierra Nevada foothills, it wants sharp drainage and some dappled shade. It is genuinely sold as both seed and nursery plant, distinguishing it from most of its rarer relatives that exist only in conservation seed banks.
